description: Statutes, rules, and cases that interact with Family Code § 1100 in community property and real estate disputes.
domain_note: Fam. Code § 1100 is a community-property management statute. Its primary home is CA_Real_Estate_Attorney (for real-estate community-property litigation). CA_Family_Law_Litigator does NOT currently build this statute (its build queue is focused on DVPA and custody statutes: Fam. §§ 6203, 6320, 6321, 6323, 3011, 3020, 3046, 3164). If CA_Family_Law_Litigator later wants to build § 1100, it should cross-reference to this canonical location.

refs.target: California Family Code § 721 (spousal fiduciary duty general rule)
refs.relationship: § 721 establishes the general spousal fiduciary duty, which § 1100(e) invokes by reference. The two must be read together.

refs.target: California Family Code § 1101 (spousal claim for breach of fiduciary duty)
refs.relationship: § 1101 provides the remedy structure for § 1100(e) breaches: (g) 50% of value + attorney's fees for ordinary breach; (h) 100% of value for breaches constituting fraud/oppression/malice under Civ. Code § 3294. Every § 1100(e) claim must be paired with § 1101.

§ 1100 governs community PERSONAL property. § 1102 governs community REAL property and requires BOTH spouses' written consent for any conveyance or encumbrance. For a house-sale case, § 1102 is the first statute to check; § 1100 applies to household furnishings and other personalty.

§ 760 establishes the presumption that property acquired during marriage is community property. This presumption is the first step in any § 1100 analysis — characterize the property, then apply the management rules.

refs.target: California Family Code § 2581 (joint title presumption at dissolution)
refs.relationship: § 2581 codifies the Lucas rule: jointly-titled property is presumed community, rebuttable only by written agreement. Relevant at dissolution for property division.

refs.target: California Family Code § 2640 (reimbursement for separate property contributions)
refs.relationship: § 2640 provides reimbursement (not ownership) for separate property contributions to community property. Codifies the Lucas rule.
§ 1101(h) explicitly incorporates Civ. Code § 3294's fraud/oppression/malice definitions. A breach of § 1100(e) that meets § 3294(c)(3) fraud gets the 100% remedy under § 1101(h).

A spouse who concealed material facts about a community property transaction is liable under § 1100(e) (spousal claim) AND under § 1572 (tort claim). Third parties who participated in the concealment are liable under § 1572 only. Both statutes should be pleaded.
